strengths: The paper proposes a simple and potentially useful post-processing approach: training-view visibility and reconstruction errors are projected onto Gaussian primitives, rendered into novel-view feature maps, and converted into pixel-wise error estimates. It applies without modifying the underlying Gaussian-splatting optimization.

The experimental study covers both RGB rendering and depth errors on 15 scenes from two datasets. It includes in-scene and cross-scene transfer, foreground/background analyses, direction-dependent representations, feature removal, linear and nonlinear regressors, AUSE and Pearson metrics, and a study of spatial context.

The strongest reported results are meaningful. With one calibration view, the 13-feature gradient-boosting model improves full-scene depth correlation over regression-FisherRF from 0.529 to 0.635 on average, and object-centric depth correlation from 0.609 to 0.790. Multi-view object-centric correlations reach approximately 0.85 for both depth and rendering error.

The regression-FisherRF comparison is informative because it subjects Fisher-derived features to the same downstream regression machinery, providing evidence that gains are attributable partly to the proposed primitive features rather than only to adding a flexible regressor.

The paper is generally understandable, and the equations provide useful definitions of the visibility, error, and direction-dependent primitive representations. Per-scene results and qualitative examples are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The claimed state-of-the-art status is not adequately supported. Despite discussing several Gaussian-splatting uncertainty methods, experiments compare only against FisherRF and a new regressed variant. The manuscript does not empirically compare against stochastic/Bayesian Gaussian-splatting methods or other recent uncertainty approaches, nor clearly establish why such comparisons are infeasible.

The work primarily evaluates correlation and sparsification, which test ranking but not whether the predicted values constitute calibrated uncertainty estimates. Since the method is explicitly trained to regress absolute error, calibration curves, coverage-risk results, NLL or another proper scoring rule, and direct MAE/RMSE of predicted error would be important. Pearson correlation is also invariant to affine scale errors, directly motivating but not resolving this concern.

Reproducibility is substantially limited. The manuscript omits exact Gaussian-splatting training and dataset preprocessing configurations, training/holdout view identities, gradient-boosting hyperparameters and pixel sampling, details of foreground-mask generation, construction of spherical-harmonic coefficients for the von Mises-Fisher representation, and runtime/memory costs. The code link remains a TBA placeholder.

The feature-selection experiment uses performance on the remaining holdout views to greedily remove features and then reports selected subsets on datasets that include those scenes. This makes the reduced-feature results partly test-set-selected and potentially optimistic. The main 13-feature results are not affected, but a disjoint validation/test protocol is needed for the feature-selection claim.

Cross-scene evidence is mixed and should be characterized more cautiously. For full-scene depth, the best combined correlations in Table 4 are only about 0.41, and some LF-trained multi-scene models are near zero or negative; the stronger transfer results largely occur after restricting evaluation to centrally segmented objects. The precise leave-one-scene-out construction is also insufficiently specified.

There are no uncertainty intervals, repeated-training variability, or scene-level significance tests. Because conclusions are drawn from only four LF and eleven TUM scenes, reporting only scene averages makes it difficult to determine whether modest differences between feature variants or regressors are reliable.

Several technical definitions need clarification: handling of primitives invisible in a training view in Eq. 5, whether viewing direction is camera-global or primitive-to-camera, approximation and possible negative values from degree-four spherical harmonics, and normalization of features and targets across scenes. Qualitative maps also lack color bars or shared-scale information, preventing assessment of their calibration. These presentation issues are secondary to the missing comparative and calibration evidence.

strengths: The core post-processing idea—projecting training-view visibility and reconstruction-error statistics onto Gaussian primitives, rendering them into novel views, and learning an error predictor—is intuitive and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers RGB and depth error, in-scene and cross-scene transfer, foreground/background regions, direction dependence, feature selection, and spatial context. The extensive per-scene appendix exposes meaningful failure cases instead of reporting only favorable aggregates.
The reported improvements over the stated FisherRF baselines are often sizable, particularly for object-centric evaluation.
weaknesses: The principal baseline may be technically mishandled. Appendix A states that diagonal Fisher-information entries correspond to variances, whereas Fisher information represents precision; covariance under the usual approximation involves the inverse Fisher matrix. The exact conversion from Fisher quantities to uncertainty is not defined. The frequently negative FisherRF correlations are consistent with a possible inversion/orientation error, so the headline comparison is not reliable as presented.

The “state-of-the-art” claim is unsupported because FisherRF and a learned FisherRF variant are the only quantitative competitors, despite the manuscript citing other recent Gaussian-splatting uncertainty methods. The experiments establish an advantage over one baseline family, not over the broader field.

The approach is primarily supervised error prediction rather than a complete uncertainty-estimation framework: fitting requires ground-truth holdout RGB or depth, while calibration, coverage, likelihood, and reliability are not evaluated. Pearson correlation is invariant to affine rescaling and does not establish meaningful uncertainty magnitudes. The authors explicitly avoid R² because target ranges shift across views, which highlights an unresolved calibration problem. AUSE is reported only for depth.

The evaluation contains only 4 LF and 11 TUM scenes, very few held-out views, and no confidence intervals or significance tests. Full-scene rendering correlations are often only about 0.2–0.4, while the strongest results come from an easier central-object setting requiring masks from an additional Gaussian Grouping pipeline.

Important protocols are unclear or potentially optimistic. The text appears inconsistent about the number of LF holdout views; feature subsets are selected on named scenes and then evaluated on “all scenes,” apparently including selection scenes; and the out-of-scene experiment does not formally specify target-scene exclusion and result aggregation. Exact splits, gradient-boosting hyperparameters, normalization, Gaussian-splatting training settings, computational cost, and masking details are missing. The code link remains “github.com/TBA.”

The direction-dependent formulation is underdefined: Eqs. 7–8 use one “direction of the view,” although Gaussian-splatting viewing direction is normally primitive-dependent. Coordinate conventions, spherical-harmonic fitting, and the degree-four implementation are not explained sufficiently for reproduction.

Cross-scene generalization is overstated: full-view transfer is often weak or negative, especially for LF-trained depth models. The qualitative figures lack common color scales or colorbars, preventing meaningful visual comparison, and several predicted maps visibly differ substantially from the true error patterns.

The conclusion reports improvements of “75.8/78.3 percentage points,” but the table values appear to support relative percentage reductions rather than absolute percentage-point gains. Numerous grammatical errors and crowded tables also reduce clarity, though these are secondary to the baseline-validity and evaluation concerns.

strengths: The paper introduces a useful and reasonably original post-processing framework: training-view visibility and reconstruction-error statistics are attached to Gaussian primitives, rendered into novel views, and combined through lightweight pixel-wise regression. This is intuitive, compatible with existing Gaussian Splatting models, and avoids modifying GS training.

The empirical improvements over FisherRF are substantial. For full-scene depth estimation, one-view AUSE decreases from 0.322 to 0.112 on LF and from 0.742 to 0.213 on TUM; multi-view variants improve further to 0.097 and 0.161. Object-centric Pearson correlations reach approximately 0.85 for both depth and rendering error.

The evaluation is unusually thorough in several dimensions: depth and RGB rendering errors, two datasets, single-view and multi-view supervision, full-scene/foreground/background regions, direction-dependent features, linear versus gradient-boosting regressors, feature selection, spatial CNN variants, and cross-scene transfer. Per-scene appendix results make important failure cases visible rather than reporting only favorable averages.

The modified regression-FisherRF baseline helps separate the benefit of the proposed representations from the benefit of supervised regression. The proposed features generally remain stronger under the same regression machinery, supporting the central technical claim.

The cross-scene experiments are practically meaningful. Although performance is moderate, multi-scene models achieve useful object-centric correlations on unseen scenes, such as combined depth correlations up to 0.667 and rendering correlations up to 0.577. This supports the claim that the features encode partially transferable error patterns.

The method is clearly motivated and the main construction is understandable. The finding that field-of-view count and visibility features are especially informative is also a useful empirical insight for future GS reliability work.
weaknesses: The claimed “state-of-the-art” status is not adequately established because the quantitative comparison is essentially limited to FisherRF and its regression-enhanced variant. Other uncertainty approaches discussed in the related work, including stochastic/Bayesian and recent view-dependent GS methods, are not evaluated. Differences in computational cost are also not reported.

Cross-scene generalization is much weaker and less universal than the framing sometimes suggests. On complete scenes, the best combined correlations in Table 4 are only about 0.409 for depth and 0.333 for rendering, and models trained on LF sometimes approach zero or negative correlation. The outdoor LF “torch” scene receives no useful transferred estimate. The evidence therefore supports moderate transfer within fairly similar object-centric circular trajectories, not broad scene-agnostic generalization.

The approach predicts supervised pixel error rather than providing a calibrated probabilistic uncertainty. It requires ground-truth holdout RGB or depth to fit an in-scene regressor, while the label-free setting depends on a regressor transferred from other scenes. This distinction and the consequences for safety-critical use should be stated more carefully; no calibration, coverage, or risk-control evaluation is provided.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The manuscript does not specify the gradient-boosting hyperparameters, GS training configuration, exact view splits and multi-scene sampling protocol, image resolutions, foreground-mask procedure, runtime, or memory overhead. The code link is still “github.com/TBA.” These omissions are material because overfitting and split composition visibly affect the results.

The evaluation reports averages without confidence intervals, repeated split variability, or statistical tests. Feature selection and model comparisons appear to use fixed small sets of holdout views, so it is difficult to judge robustness to the selected regression view. Pixel-wise samples within an image are highly dependent and should not be interpreted as independent statistical evidence.

Some technical definitions need tightening. Equations 4–5 aggregate over all views even though a primitive may be invisible and the corresponding pixel set can be empty; the treatment of such cases is unspecified. The direction used in the von Mises–Fisher representation should be defined explicitly per primitive, and the appendix imprecisely describes Fisher-information diagonal entries as parameter variances rather than information whose inverse approximates covariance.

The conclusion describes AUSE reductions as “percentage points,” although the reported 75.8% and 78.3% figures appear to be relative reductions. Qualitative maps also lack shared color bars or numerical scales, making their magnitudes difficult to compare. These are presentation issues rather than reasons for rejection.

strengths: PRIMU offers a useful and reasonably original post-hoc formulation: training-view coverage and reconstruction errors are projected onto Gaussian primitives, rendered as feature maps, and converted into dense error estimates without retraining the underlying Gaussian-splatting model.

The empirical results are strong across several datasets. With one held-out view, PRIMU improves both AUSE and Pearson correlation over FisherRF, manifold sampling, and var3DGS for RGB-error estimation, and over BayesRays, FisherRF, and manifold sampling for depth-error estimation.

The evaluation is broader than a single headline comparison. It includes direction-dependent features, foreground/background separation, linear versus gradient-boosting regressors, different numbers of supervision views, feature-subset analysis, cross-scene transfer, spatial CNN variants, and an active-view-selection application.

The regression-based FisherRF comparison is informative because it partially separates the benefit of supervised error regression from the quality of PRIMU's proposed primitive features; PRIMU remains better in the reported matched-regression settings.

The method is conceptually interpretable, and the manuscript is generally clear. Qualitative examples support the quantitative finding that PRIMU maps track important error regions more closely than the baseline maps.
weaknesses: The strongest uncertainty-estimation results require ground-truth observations from a held-out view of each scene. A single image still supplies a very large number of supervised pixel targets, so the repeated characterization as limited supervision should be interpreted cautiously. This requirement also reduces applicability in settings where uncertainty is needed precisely because additional ground truth cannot be acquired.

The main state-of-the-art tables do not provide fully controlled comparisons: PRIMU uses a learned gradient-boosting calibration stage, whereas several baselines use their native uncertainty outputs and, for stochastic methods, different underlying reconstructions. The regression-controlled FisherRF study helps, but it is confined to LF/TUM scene-separation experiments and does not establish the same conclusion against manifold or var3DGS under matched calibration.

The claim that cross-scene models enable uncertainty estimation without new hold-out data is only partially supported. Table 8 contains useful object-centric transfer results, but performance for entire scenes and backgrounds is often modest, near zero, or negative—especially for LF depth and some direction-dependent configurations. The paper's broad deployment claim should therefore be restricted to particular datasets and regions.

The work primarily evaluates error ranking or correlation rather than calibrated predictive uncertainty. AUSE and Pearson correlation are appropriate for localization and triage, but they do not show whether predicted magnitudes have probabilistic meaning or are calibrated. This distinction matters given the safety-critical motivation.

Statistical evidence is limited: results are reported mainly as dataset means without per-scene dispersion, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed variability. This is particularly important for the active-view-selection gain, which is demonstrated only through one averaged table and is relatively modest over FisherRF, with no robustness analysis.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are absent or underspecified, including gradient-boosting hyperparameters and pixel sampling, exact hold-out/evaluation-view selection, the procedure used to approximate direction-dependent representations with degree-four spherical harmonics, runtime and storage costs, and a complete list of the selected TUM scenes. These are correctable reporting deficiencies rather than flaws in the central idea.

strengths: The central idea—projecting training-view coverage and reconstruction-error statistics onto Gaussian primitives and rendering them as features—is intuitive, interpretable, and technically relevant to Gaussian Splatting.

The method is post-hoc and avoids retraining the underlying splat representation. The paper explores direction-dependent features, foreground/background separation, feature subsets, linear versus gradient-boosting regressors, and limited cross-scene transfer.
On the reported same-scene experiments, PRIMU substantially improves AUSE and Pearson correlation over the evaluated baselines, particularly for depth and object-centric regions.
The active-view-selection application is useful and improves all three reported reconstruction metrics over FisherRF and manifold under the adopted MipNeRF360 protocol.
weaknesses: The main state-of-the-art comparison is materially confounded by supervision. PRIMU is trained using dense ground-truth rendering or depth errors from a hold-out view of each target scene, whereas the principal baselines in Tables 1–2 do not receive equivalent labeled target-scene data. This makes the headline conclusion that the primitive features themselves outperform prior uncertainty methods unsupported. The regression-based FisherRF control is informative but is only reported in the separate scene-separation study, not in the main benchmark.

Requiring a ground-truth hold-out view weakens the claimed safety-critical and novel-view utility: in many deployment settings, the true image—and especially true depth—needed to train the regressor is precisely unavailable. The cross-scene experiment could address this limitation, but its results are much weaker than the same-scene results. For example, whole-scene rendering correlations in Table 8 are generally only around 0.1–0.33, and several background/depth settings are near zero or negative. Thus the broad claim of uncertainty estimation without additional hold-out data is overstated.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates across scenes, random seeds, and view choices. Only dataset averages are reported, with no per-scene results, dispersion, or significance analysis. This is consequential for the small active-view-selection gain over FisherRF (20.721 versus 20.392 PSNR) and does not support the claim that the method “reliably” surpasses the baselines.

The active-view-selection evidence is incomplete. It covers only MipNeRF360 and 20 selected views, omits basic random, fixed-spacing, and farthest-view controls, and provides no ablation validating the chosen coverage feature or direction-dependent formulation. Consequently, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed uncertainty representation rather than a competitive coverage heuristic or experimental variance.

Several comparisons are not directly controlled: BayesRays uses a different NeRF representation, while manifold and var3DGS alter the underlying GS model and consequently its error distribution. Reporting reconstruction quality helps expose this issue but does not make AUSE and correlation comparisons fully comparable. A consistent regressor applied to features from all methods on identical splats would better isolate the contribution.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including gradient-boosting hyperparameters and pixel sampling, precise hold-out/test-view selection, the number of views denoted by “m-view,” fitting and rendering details for the spherical-harmonic approximation of the von Mises–Fisher features, and complete AUSE computation and aggregation procedures. The feature-selection study also does not clearly separate the views used to select feature combinations from those used for final evaluation, leaving possible model-selection leakage.

The method’s novelty is moderate: it combines handcrafted visibility/error statistics, standard splatting, and off-the-shelf supervised regression. The extensive ablations are useful, but the current experimental design does not establish that this combination constitutes a calibrated or generally transferable uncertainty estimator rather than a scene-specific error predictor.

There are secondary presentation issues—such as “maniflod,” “Gaoli,” “Leaned Perceptual,” inconsistent descriptions of qualitative outputs as feature maps versus predicted uncertainty, and a depth-figure caption referring to rendering error—but these are refinements rather than the basis of the rating.

strengths: PRIMU offers a useful and reasonably original post-hoc formulation: training-view coverage and reconstruction errors are projected onto Gaussian primitives, rendered into interpretable feature maps, and converted into pixel-level error estimates without retraining the underlying Gaussian Splatting model.

The empirical results are strong. With one hold-out view, PRIMU substantially improves rendering-error AUSE over the reported baselines on LF (0.286 versus 0.435 or worse), MipNeRF360 (0.378 versus 0.520 or worse), and LLFF (0.281 versus 0.476 or worse). Its LF depth-error correlation of 0.728 is also markedly higher than BayesRays (0.243) and FisherRF (0.105).

The evaluation is broader than a single headline table: it covers four datasets, color and depth errors, foreground/background separation, direction-dependent features, linear versus gradient-boosting regressors, feature-subset ablations, cross-scene transfer, and qualitative comparisons.

The regression-controlled comparison is informative. When FisherRF features are given the same gradient-boosting machinery, PRIMU still performs better across the principal scene-separation settings, supporting the claim that its primitive features—not only the regressor—are useful.

The active-view-selection application is practical and does not require a hold-out view or trained error regressor. Under the adopted MipNeRF360 protocol, it improves all three reconstruction metrics over FisherRF and manifold, reaching 20.721 PSNR, 0.625 SSIM, and 0.340 LPIPS.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and the visual results indicate that PRIMU maps localize actual error structure more faithfully than the compared raw uncertainty maps.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons are not completely controlled: PRIMU uses supervised pixel-wise regression on ground-truth errors from a hold-out view, whereas the principal baselines in Tables 1–2 are used without equivalent calibration. The regression-based FisherRF study partly addresses this concern, but only on LF/TUM scene-separation experiments rather than the main MipNeRF360/LLFF benchmarks.

The method primarily predicts absolute reconstruction error rather than a probabilistic uncertainty distribution. Evaluation is limited to AUSE and Pearson correlation, with no calibration error, prediction intervals, negative log-likelihood, or coverage-versus-risk analysis. Consequently, the safety-critical motivation is stronger than the evidence actually provided.

The abstract's claim that cross-scene generalization enables use without additional hold-out data is too broad. Table 8 shows good transfer mainly for object-centric cases; several entire-scene and background settings have weak correlations, including near-zero or negative depth correlations for LF-trained models. This limitation should be stated prominently.

The active-view-selection evidence is promising but narrow: it uses one dataset and one protocol, reports modest gains over FisherRF, includes no random or camera-coverage heuristic baseline, and provides neither variability across runs nor per-scene results. Thus, the claim of reliably superior selection is not yet strongly established.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including gradient-boosting hyperparameters, pixel sampling and preprocessing, exact hold-out/multi-view splits, per-scene sample counts, depth-rendering conventions, computational cost, and sensitivity to the visibility thresholds, kappa, and spherical-harmonic truncation. No code-release statement is apparent.

Results are presented almost entirely as dataset averages without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or per-scene values. This makes it difficult to determine whether the improvements—especially the active-view-selection and direction-dependent gains—are consistent or driven by particular scenes.

There are minor presentation issues, including typographical errors and an incorrect constant in the stated three-dimensional von Mises–Fisher density normalization. The latter appears inconsequential because the density is subsequently rescaled to unit maximum, but it should still be corrected.
